title: LLM Uncertainty at Millions-of-Users Scale
reported: AI Engineer interview (no DSA): how would you handle LLM uncertainty when serving millions of users?

sources.passage:
Fposts%2Fjohan-abhishek-dasari_aiengineering-swiggy-agenticai-activity-7443590338931314688-Ni3Z&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

I gave an interview at [Swiggy](https://in.linkedin.com/company/swiggy-in?trk=public_post-text) for an AI Engineer role recently.

And some of you might be surprised by what they actually ask.

No DSA. No backend trivia. No system design in the traditional sense.

Instead:

"How would you solve LLM uncertainty at millions of users scale?"
"How do you evaluate if your agent is actually working correctly?"
"What is LLM-as-judge and when would you use it?"
"How do you stop your agent from hallucinating a successful order when the tool call failed?"

Think about that last one for a second.

They're not asking if you can build an agent. They're asking if you understand what happens when it breaks — at scale, in production, with real money and real orders on the line.

AI engineering at a company like Swiggy isn't about which framework you used. It's about solving problems so vulnerable that a wrong answer doesn't just crash an app — it puts orders, payments, and trust at risk for millions of people.

That's a completely different level of thinking.

But if you're preparing for AI engineering roles in 2026, forget LeetCode for a minute and go deep on:
→ Evals and how to measure agent quality
→ LLM-as-judge pattern
→ Fault tolerance in agentic systems
→ How you'd handle uncertainty at scale

The bar is higher than most people think. And way more interesting.

### Interview Experience

The entire process took about 8 weeks from the initial recruiter call to the final offer rollout. The interview loop consisted of three main rounds evaluating core problem-solving, design capability, and engineering experience.

---

#### Round 1: External Bar Raiser (60 Mins)

I was provided with a static dataset and basic HTML structure.

I approached the problem step by step:

#### 1. Reusable Render Function

I first created a reusable function that takes a list of items and renders them as cards on the UI.

#### 2. Central Filtering Logic

Then I implemented a central function (`applyFilter`) which:

* Reads input values from search, filter, and sort dropdowns

* Applies sorting using JavaScript’s `sort()` function

I ensured that all filters work **together**, so the UI updates correctly when multiple inputs change.

I added event listeners on:

* Search input
* Sort dropdown
* Filter dropdown
